title: Chicken two ways
skill: Using every part of one bird, costed

notes.text: For more than 6, break down two chickens, pan-roast the breasts in two skillets, and use the stockpot for both backs and all four legs.

move.title: One bird, two dinners, one price
move.body: This is the unit's mastery week, on your own: one whole chicken, broken down and used completely. The breasts are pan-roasted skin side down and finished in the oven. The legs, wings, and back simmer into a stock, and the stock and leg meat become a chicken noodle soup. At the end you work out what each serving cost from the receipt.

why.title: Plan backward
why.body: The soup takes longest, so the stock starts first and simmers while you do everything else. The breasts go in the pan last, so they come out hot when the soup is ready.

why.title: Stock starts cold
why.body: Bones and meat started in cold water release their proteins slowly, which rise as foam you can skim. Started in boiling water, the proteins scatter and cloud the stock.

why.title: Never boil stock
why.body: A hard boil churns fat and proteins into the liquid and turns it cloudy and greasy. Keep it to a lazy simmer, a bubble or two breaking the surface.

why.title: Skin side down, then the oven
why.body: A breast seared skin side down in a hot pan gets crisp, golden skin. The oven finishes the thick meat evenly, so the outside doesn't dry out while the middle catches up.

why.title: Cost per serving
why.body: Add up what you spent on everything the two dishes used, from the receipt, and divide by the servings you got. Compare it with buying breasts and a carton of stock.

wrong.fix: It boiled. It's still good to eat; next time, keep it at a bare simmer and skim the foam early.
Simmer it uncovered another 20 minutes to concentrate it, then salt it.

wrong.sign: The breast skin stuck and tore
wrong.fix: It wasn't ready to release. Wait until it lets go on its own.
They sat in the hot soup. Next time, cook them in the soup just before serving, or store them apart.

quiz.q: Why does the stock start in cold water?
choices: Proteins release slowly and rise as foam you can skim

quiz.explain: A lazy simmer keeps it clear.

quiz.q: The ingredients cost $18.60 and made 6 servings of each dish. What's the cost per serving?

steps.text: Read the recipe through and write your timeline backward from serving: stock first, soup next, breasts last.
steps.tip: This is the mastery check. Plan it and cook it on your own.

steps.text: Weigh the chicken and keep the receipt.

Break the chicken down: breasts off the bone with the skin on, legs off at the hip, wings off at the shoulder, and the back in 3 pieces. Season the breasts with the chicken's salt and pepper and refrigerate them.
steps.look: Two skin-on breasts, two whole legs, two wings, and the back.

steps.text: Put the legs, wings, and back in the stockpot with the stock's cold water.
Wash your hands, the knife, and the board with hot, soapy water.
Cut the stock's onion, carrots, and celery into 2-inch chunks, no need to peel, and add them with the bay, peppercorns, and thyme.
Bring the stock just to a simmer over medium-high, skim the foam, then turn it down to a lazy simmer, uncovered.
Lift out a leg: the thickest part of the thigh should read at least 165°F and pull from the bone. Move the legs to the plate.
Once cool enough to touch, pull the leg meat off the bones in bite-size pieces. Return the bones and skin to the pot.
Strain the stock through the colander into the large bowl. Measure it and skim off the fat.
steps.look: About 2 quarts of clear, golden stock.

steps.text: Dice the soup's onion, carrots, and celery into ½-inch pieces.
Heat the oven to 400°F with the sheet pan inside.
Bring the stock to a simmer in the large pot, add the diced vegetables and the soup's salt, and simmer until tender.
Heat the oil in the skillet over medium-high. Lay the breasts in skin side down with the tongs.
Wash the tongs and your hands.
Sear without moving until the skin is golden and releases, then move them, skin side up, to the hot sheet pan in the oven.
Check the thickest breast: at least 165°F. Rest them 5 minutes.
Add the noodles and shredded leg meat to the soup and simmer until the noodles are tender. Stir in the parsley and taste for salt.
Check the soup: at least 165°F.
Slice the breasts across the grain. Serve them with the soup, or the soup as tonight's dinner and the breasts as tomorrow's.
From the receipt, add up the cost of everything you used and divide by the number of servings you made. Write the cost per serving.
